main_damage_causes: Lee Jordan's distinctive partisan, humorous commentary voice is replaced with neutral functional announcing, eliminating his defining personality trait
The recurring comedic McGonagall-Jordan dynamic, central to his book characterisation across multiple matches, is entirely absent from the film

The film corpus is limited to two Quidditch scenes from Philosopher's Stone, meaning the richer later portrayals (OotP Quidditch matches, Potterwatch, Battle of Hogwarts) cannot be assessed — the damage identified is likely a floor, not a ceiling

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Lee Jordan's commentary during the first Quidditch match
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Lee Jordan's commentary is vivid, partisan, funny, and frequently interrupted by Professor McGonagall for bias. He gives detailed, colourful play-by-play, editorialises about players' looks ('rather attractive, too'), gets progressively more furious at Slytherin cheating ('YOU FILTHY, CHEATING B--'), and is a distinct comedic voice who pushes the boundaries of what McGonagall will tolerate. His personality is defined by irreverence, wit, and fierce Gryffindor loyalty expressed through escalating verbal transgression.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Lee Jordan delivers only functional, neutral announcements: 'Angelina Johnson scores! 10 points for Gryffindor!', 'Slytherin takes possession of the Quaffle. Bletchley passes to Captain Marcus Flint.' He also straightforwardly announces 'He's got the Snitch! Harry Potter receives 150 points for catching the Snitch!' There is no bias, no humour, no McGonagall interventions, no escalating outrage at Slytherin fouls. He functions as a scoreboard announcer rather than a character.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses Lee's commentary as characterisation — his partisan wit and McGonagall's exasperated corrections are a running comic thread across multiple Quidditch scenes. The film strips this entirely, reducing him to a neutral PA system. His distinct voice, the comedic McGonagall-Jordan dynamic, and his role as an enthusiastic, boundary-pushing personality are all lost. This matters because his commentary style is one of the primary ways the books establish him as a character rather than a background fixture.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Absence of McGonagall-Jordan comedic dynamic during match
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 11 and 17-19 establish a recurring comedic relationship: McGonagall repeatedly growls 'JORDAN!' and warns Lee off his biased commentary, while Lee apologises and immediately resumes editorialising. This is a distinct, recurring interpersonal dynamic that gives McGonagall a rare moment of exasperated informality and gives Lee relational definition.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: McGonagall does not interact with Lee Jordan at all during the match commentary. The dynamic is entirely absent. There is no 'JORDAN!', no warning, no apology-followed-by-resumption.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The McGonagall-Jordan back-and-forth is a small but recurring relationship beat that humanises both characters. Its absence means Lee loses his most defining relational context in the film, and McGonagall loses a moment of comedic warmth. For a character with limited screen time, losing his primary interpersonal dynamic is proportionally significant.
